pos: n. (John Purvey, c. 1354–c. 1414, Wycliffe's secretary and reviser of the Lollard Bible)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Purvey, from Old French porveoir, to provide, to furnish.
biblical_def: John Purvey was Wycliffe's secretary at Lutterworth in his last years and is generally held to be the man behind the second and far better version of the Wycliffite English Bible. The first version had followed the Latin word for word, so closely that the English is often unreadable; the revision rewrites it into the idiom of the language, and the prologue sets out the translator's method — gather the best Latin copies, settle the text, consult the glosses, take counsel of men learned in the tongue, and translate the sentence rather than the words. That prologue is the first serious statement of translation principle in English and it is still sound. Purvey was imprisoned, recanted under pressure in 1401, was given a living, resigned it, and seems to have been in prison again at the end. The recantation is part of the record and should not be hidden. So is the Bible, which outlived both the recantation and the men who extorted it. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines idiom as a mode of expression peculiar to a language, and recant as to retract a declaration or proposition, to unsay.
webster_full: ID'IOM, n. A mode of expression peculiar to a language; a peculiarity of expression or phraseology.
RECANT', v. To retract a declaration or proposition; to unsay what has been said; to recall.
PRO'LOGUE, n. A preface or introduction to a discourse or performance.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
corruption_summary: Wycliffe's secretary, the second English Bible, and a recantation in the record.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the handling of a recantation as though it cancelled the work. Purvey broke under examination in 1401 and the Lollards never fully trusted him afterwards. The revised Bible went on circulating in hundreds of manuscripts for a century and a half, copied by hand at real risk, long after everyone had forgotten who revised it.

The principle to recover is that the endurance of the word does not rest on the endurance of the men who handle it. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is a contrast between two kinds of thing, and the translator is on the grass side of it. Paul's warning stands over the whole business and over every reader of it: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).

pos: n. (Nicholas Hereford, d. c. 1420, Oxford Wycliffite and translator of the first English Bible)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; English Hereford, from the city, the army ford.
biblical_def: Nicholas Hereford was a doctor of divinity of Oxford and the most prominent academic Wycliffite of his generation, and the manuscript evidence identifies him as the translator of a large part of the Old Testament in the first Wycliffite version — one surviving copy breaks off in the middle of Baruch with a note that this is where Hereford's hand stopped, probably where his summons to London interrupted him. He was excommunicated, went to Rome to appeal, was condemned and imprisoned there, escaped during a rising, came home, was imprisoned again, and in 1391 recanted. He then turned and prosecuted his former associates with the vigour of a man proving something, became chancellor of Hereford cathedral, and finally retired into a Carthusian house at Coventry to die. His is the completest reversal in the Lollard story. The translation he did before the break is still the translation he did. “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed, and excommunication as the act of ejecting from a church.
webster_full: APOS'TASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
EXCOMMUNICA'TION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from its communion.
RECANTA'TION, n. Retraction; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
CHAN'CELLOR, n. A judicial officer; in cathedral churches, an officer who hears causes and keeps the records.
scriptures: Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: The Oxford doctor who translated half the Old Testament and then prosecuted his own friends.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a sentimentality about defectors that insists every reversal must be explained by pressure, fear or poor treatment. Hereford was pressed severely and imprisoned twice, and after he turned he did not merely retire into silence; he took an active part in hunting the men he had worked with. The record carries both the translation and the prosecutions.

The principle to recover is John's, which is the hardest sentence in the New Testament on this subject and is given as an explanation rather than a lament: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us” (1Jo 2:19). Continuance is the evidence. Paul's warning applies to the confident onlooker as much as to the man who fell: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).

pos: n. (William Sawtrey, d. 1401, parish priest of Lynn, the first Lollard burned in England)
etymology: Germanic William, resolute protector; English Sawtrey, from a Huntingdonshire place-name.
biblical_def: William Sawtrey was a parish priest of Lynn in Norfolk who was examined for heresy in 1399, abjured, and then went on preaching the same things in London. In February 1401 he was tried again, condemned as a relapsed heretic, degraded from his orders, and burned at Smithfield — the first man put to death for heresy in England under the new procedure, and the first of the Lollards to die that way. The statute that made the burning of heretics the law of England, the De heretico comburendo, was passing through parliament at the same moment; the writ for Sawtrey was issued before the act received assent, so the law caught up with the fire. The articles against him were that he would not adore the cross, that he held a priest should preach rather than say the canonical hours, and that the bread after consecration remains bread. On the last of these he was burned. “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heretic as one who holds an opinion contrary to the established faith, and abjure as to renounce upon oath.
webster_full: HER'ETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the Christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
ABJU'RE, v. To renounce upon oath; to abandon; to reject with solemnity.
RELAPSE', v. To slide or turn back into a former state or practice; to fall back.
DEGRADA'TION, n. A reducing in rank; deposition; the act of depriving of an office or dignity.
scriptures: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: The parish priest of Lynn, burned at Smithfield before the statute that allowed it had passed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the treatment of the medieval heresy burnings as a procedural excess of a violent age rather than as the defence of a specific doctrine. The articles against Sawtrey are on the record and they are doctrinal: the adoration of the cross, the duty of preaching, and above all whether the bread remains bread. He was burned for denying transubstantiation, which is what the proceedings say.

The principle to recover is the arithmetic the Lord gives his disciples before he sends them out, which is the only calculation that makes a Smithfield rational. “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28). The limit of the magistrate's power is stated in the verse. Peter states the corresponding duty: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and John describes the outcome from the other side: they “loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).

pos: n. (John Badby, d. 1410, Worcestershire tailor burned for denying transubstantiation)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Badby, from a Northamptonshire place-name.
biblical_def: John Badby was a tailor or blacksmith of Evesham, an unlettered layman, tried before Archbishop Arundel in 1410 for saying that the consecrated host is not the body of Christ but bread, and that if every host were the Lord's body there would be twenty thousand gods in England. He would not retract. He was burned at Smithfield in a barrel. The Prince of Wales, afterwards Henry V, was present and had the fire pulled apart when he heard the man cry out, offering him his life and a pension if he would recant; Badby, on his feet again, refused, and the barrel was replaced over him. The scene is reported by chroniclers hostile to him, which is what makes it so difficult to argue with. A tradesman who could not read held a position about the sacrament against an archbishop and a prince and chose the fire twice. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines host as the consecrated wafer in the Roman church, and constancy as firmness of mind, unalterable continuance.
webster_full: HOST, n. In the Romish church, the sacrifice of the mass, or the consecrated wafer, offered as an expiation for the sins of the living and the dead.
CON'STANCY, n. Firmness of mind; a steady, unshaken determination; unalterable continuance.
AR'TISAN, n. One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman.
PEN'SION, n. An annual allowance of a sum of money to a person by government.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
corruption_summary: The Evesham tradesman who refused his life twice in the fire at Smithfield.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the condescension that treats a layman's doctrinal stand as stubbornness, since he had no learning with which to weigh the question. The chroniclers who recorded Badby took that line and the record defeats them anyway. He had grasped the one thing that mattered and could state it: the bread remains bread, and what is multiplied on ten thousand altars is not the body of the Lord.

The principle to recover is that God has deliberately arranged the confounding of the learned by the unlearned, and says so. “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27). Luke records the Sanhedrin discovering the same thing: “they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13).

pos: n. (William Swinderby, fl. 1382–1392, Lollard preacher of Leicester and the Welsh march)
etymology: Germanic William, resolute protector; English Swinderby, from a Lincolnshire place-name.
biblical_def: William Swinderby was a hermit near Leicester who began preaching about 1382, first against the pride and dress of women, then against the friars, then on the Wycliffite articles. He was forbidden the churches and preached from a chapel in the woods, and when that was shut he preached from a pulpit built against a disused chapel outside the walls so that his hearers stood on common ground where the bishop had no hold. Driven out of Leicester, he went to Herefordshire and the Welsh march and preached there for years with the protection of sympathetic gentry. He was tried before the bishop of Hereford in 1391, submitted articles in writing that conceded nothing of substance, and was finally condemned; what became of him is not known, and there is no record of a burning. He is the type of the itinerant Lollard preacher, the man without a benefice preaching on the edge of parishes. “And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amo 7:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itinerant as passing or travelling from place to place, and hermit as a person who retires from society and lives in solitude.
webster_full: ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling from place to place; not settled; applied to preachers who travel.
HER'MIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse.
BEN'EFICE, n. In church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.
CON'VENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; appropriately, a secret assembly or meeting for worship.
scriptures: Amo 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: The hermit of Leicester who preached from common ground when the churches were shut.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that an unlicensed preacher is by that fact a disorderly one, which was the whole weight of the case against Swinderby and is a serious argument that deserves a serious answer. The church's order is real and Scripture requires it. But a licence withheld in order to silence the word is not order, and a pulpit built on common ground is a judgment on the authority that shut the building.

The principle to recover is Amos's answer to the priest who told him to go and prophesy somewhere else. He does not claim a licence; he claims a commission, and distinguishes the two: “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit” (Amo 7:14), and then the reason he is standing there: “the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel” (Amo 7:15). Jeremiah describes the inward compulsion: “I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jer 20:9).

pos: n. (Sir John Oldcastle, Lord Cobham, c. 1378–1417, Lollard knight)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Oldcastle, from a Herefordshire place-name.
biblical_def: Sir John Oldcastle was a soldier of the Welsh march, a friend of Henry V from the Welsh campaigns, and Lord Cobham by marriage, and he was the most powerful layman the Lollards ever had. He protected their preachers on his lands, distributed their books, and when he was accused in 1413 he answered the archbishop to his face on the sacrament and on confession, was condemned, escaped from the Tower, and in January 1414 attempted a rising at St Giles's Fields that was betrayed and scattered before it began. He was hunted for three years, taken in Wales, and hanged over a fire at St Giles's in 1417, executed as a traitor and burned as a heretic in one motion. The rising is the thing to be plain about. Whatever the provocation, an armed attempt against the king was rebellion, and Scripture gives the subject no such remedy. It also destroyed the Lollard cause as a public movement and left it to survive underground for a century. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines insurrection as a rising against civil authority, and treason as the highest crime of a civil nature, a betraying of the sovereign or state.
webster_full: INSURREC'TION, n. A rising against civil or political authority; the open and active opposition of a number of persons to the execution of law.
TREA'SON, n. The highest crime of a civil nature of which a man can be guilty; disloyalty; betraying of a trust.
KNIGHT, n. Originally a youth; afterward, a young man admitted to the privilege of bearing arms.
REBEL'LION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
corruption_summary: The Lollard knight whose rising destroyed the movement he meant to save.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the enlistment of Oldcastle as a proto-revolutionary, a Protestant hero whose rebellion was the gospel applied to politics. That reading is as old as the sixteenth century and was pressed by men who should have known better. It will not do. The attempt at St Giles's Fields was armed rebellion against the lawful king, and it had exactly the effect such attempts have: it handed the authorities a security argument against every Lollard in England.

The principle to recover is that the subject's duty is stated without an exception for a righteous cause. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1); “Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake” (1Pe 2:13). Peter wrote that under Nero. The Lord's word in the garden settles the method for his followers once and for all: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52), which is also, precisely, what happened at St Giles's.

pos: n. pl. (the Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards, 1395, presented to parliament)
etymology: Latin duodecim, twelve; conclusio, a shutting up, an inference, a settled judgment.
biblical_def: The Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards were nailed to the doors of Westminster Hall and St Paul's in 1395 while parliament sat, a manifesto in English addressed to the lords and commons of the realm. They charge that the English church has been corrupted by its endowment; that the priesthood as then constituted is not that of the New Testament; that clerical celibacy breeds uncleanness; that transubstantiation leads the people into idolatry; that the blessing of oil, salt and water is a kind of necromancy; that holding secular office alongside a cure of souls is unlawful; that prayers for the dead sold for money corrupt charity; that pilgrimage and the veneration of images are near to idolatry; that auricular confession to a priest exalts him above his place; that killing in war and by judicial sentence without plain warrant is against the New Testament; that vows of continence laid on women lead to great sin; and that the multitude of unnecessary crafts in the realm feeds pride. They are uneven. Several of them are the Reformation stated a hundred and twenty years early. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines manifesto as a public declaration of the reasons for a proceeding, and conclusion as an inference, a final judgment or determination.
webster_full: MANIFES'TO, n. A public declaration, usually of a prince or sovereign, showing his intentions and the reasons of his proceedings.
CONCLU'SION, n. The inference that is drawn from premises; a final judgment or determination.
ENDOW'MENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a church.
IDOL'ATRY, n. The worship of idols, images or anything made by hands, or which is not God.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: A manifesto nailed to Westminster Hall in 1395, uneven, and in places the Reformation early.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reading of the Conclusions as a uniformly admirable document because several of its articles anticipate the Reformation. They are uneven and should be said to be. The eleventh, on vows of continence, is handled coarsely; the twelfth, against unnecessary crafts, is a social complaint with little scriptural warrant; the tenth comes close to denying the magistrate the sword that Romans 13 gives him.

The principle to recover is the test the Conclusions themselves appeal to and which judges them as well: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Measured by it, the articles on images and on the mediator stand where the document is strongest. The second commandment is explicit (Exo 20:4), and the New Testament leaves one mediator and no other: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).

pos: n. (Philip Repyngdon, c. 1345–1424, Oxford Wycliffite, afterwards bishop of Lincoln)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; English Repyngdon, from the Derbyshire place-name Repton.
biblical_def: Philip Repyngdon was an Augustinian canon and a doctor of Oxford who in 1382 preached publicly in defence of Wycliffe's teaching on the sacrament and was excommunicated for it. Within months he had submitted, and his rise from that point was uninterrupted: abbot of Leicester, chancellor of Oxford, confessor to Henry IV, bishop of Lincoln in 1405, and cardinal. As bishop he proceeded against Lollards in his own diocese, the diocese in which Wycliffe had held his last living and Swinderby had preached. He is also on record rebuking the king sharply for misgovernment, which complicates the picture without redeeming it. Repyngdon is the clearest case in the whole Lollard story of the reward attached to recantation and the cost attached to constancy, and the two men to set beside him are Sawtrey and Badby, who were burned in the years he was rising. A church that makes submission profitable will get a great many submissions. “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mar 8:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preferment as advancement to a higher office or dignity, and temporize as to comply with the time or prevailing opinion.
webster_full: PREFER'MENT, n. Advancement to a higher office, dignity or station; promotion.
TEM'PORIZE, v. To comply with the time or occasion; to humor or yield to the current of opinion or to circumstances.
CHAN'CELLOR, n. In England, the chief officer of a university.
CON'FESSOR, n. A priest who hears the confession of others and has power to grant absolution.
scriptures: Mar 8:36
For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Mar 8:38

Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
corruption_summary: The Oxford Wycliffite who submitted, rose to a bishopric, and prosecuted Lollards in his own diocese.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern description of such a career as a change of mind, with the implication that any further judgment is presumption. Men do change their minds and some of Repyngdon's later conduct suggests he kept a conscience. But the shape of the record cannot be set aside: he defended Wycliffe, submitted, and every promotion in the English church followed the submission, while the men who held the same position he had abandoned were being burned.

The principle to recover is the exchange rate the Lord states, which is the only one that makes sense of a Smithfield or a mitre. “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mar 8:36). He attaches the warning directly to being ashamed of his words in a hostile generation (Mar 8:38). Solomon names the mechanism without any drama at all: “The fear of man bringeth a snare” (Pro 29:25).

pos: n. (Richard Wyche, d. 1440, Lollard priest burned on Tower Hill)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong in rule; English Wyche, from Old English wic, a dwelling or a salt-works.
biblical_def: Richard Wyche was a priest of the north of England who was examined for Lollardy about 1402 by the bishop of Durham, imprisoned, and wrote from prison a long letter describing the examination — one of the very few first-person accounts of a heresy trial from the accused's own hand in that century. He describes the pressure, the shifting of the articles, the offers, and his own vacillation with a candour that nobody writing propaganda would have allowed himself. He conformed eventually and was released. He also corresponded with Jan Hus in Bohemia, and Hus read his letter aloud to the congregation at Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, which is a thread worth holding: an English Lollard in a Durham prison and a Czech reformer in Prague encouraging each other across the continent twenty years before the Hussite wars. Wyche was finally burned on Tower Hill in 1440, nearly forty years after his first trial. Londoners gathered at the place of his burning for weeks afterwards until the authorities stopped them. “And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony” (Rev 12:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines examination as a judicial inquiry by interrogation, and correspondence as intercourse between persons at a distance by letters.
webster_full: EXAMINA'TION, n. A careful search or inquiry; in judicial proceedings, a careful inquiry into facts by testimony.
CORRESPOND'ENCE, n. Intercourse between persons at a distance, by means of letters sent and answers received.
PRIS'ON, n. A public building for the confinement or safe custody of debtors and criminals.
EPIS'TLE, n. A writing directed or sent to a person; a letter.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Col 4:18
The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: The Lollard priest who wrote his own trial from prison and corresponded with Jan Hus.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy martyr narrative, in which the accused is composed throughout and the only drama is the fire. Wyche's own letter refuses that shape. He records his wavering, the formulas he was willing to sign and the ones he was not, and the fact that he conformed in the end and went free. He was burned thirty-eight years later, having lived a long ordinary life in between.

The principle to recover is that Scripture commands a particular act of imagination toward prisoners which the tidy narrative makes impossible: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3). As bound with them — which means reckoning with the fear, not admiring the courage from outside. Paul's own three-word postscript does the same work: “Remember my bonds” (Col 4:18).

pos: n. (John Claydon, d. 1415, London currier burned with his books)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Claydon, from a place-name, the clay hill.
biblical_def: John Claydon was a currier of London — a dresser of tanned leather — who could not read, and who was burned at Smithfield in 1415 for owning a book. He had been imprisoned for Lollardy years before and released on submission. In 1415 his house was searched and officers took away English books, among them a handsomely bound volume called The Lantern of Light, which Claydon had paid to have copied and bound and which he had had read aloud to him and to others in his house. At his trial the book was read out and condemned, and he was condemned with it, as a relapsed heretic. The book was burned with him. It is a very exact picture of what the authorities were actually afraid of. Not a theologian, not a preacher, not a rising: a leather-dresser who could not read, who had bought a book and had it read aloud in his parlour to his household and his neighbours. “Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy” (Rev 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines currier as one who dresses and colors leather after it is tanned, and illiterate as unlettered, ignorant of letters.
webster_full: CUR'RIER, n. A man who dresses and colors leather, after it is tanned.
ILLIT'ERATE, a. Unlettered; ignorant of letters or books; untaught; unlearned.
CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly for religious worship; appropriately, a secret or unlawful assembly.
BIND, v. To cover a book with leather or other material, and fasten the leaves.
scriptures: Rev 1:3
Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand.
Col 4:16
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.
I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren.
Luk 4:16
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
corruption_summary: The London leather-dresser who could not read and was burned with his book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the picture of medieval Bible-reading as an individual affair, a man alone with a text, which makes Claydon's case hard to see. He could not read at all. What he had was a book, a household, and somebody willing to read it aloud; and that arrangement — one copy, one reader, a room full of hearers — is how the word reached most people in every century before the last two, including the apostolic one.

The principle to recover is that Scripture pronounces its blessing on the reader and the hearers together, which assumes exactly that room. “Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy” (Rev 1:3). Paul gives the corresponding charge in the strongest form he has: “I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren” (1Th 5:27). The Lord himself stood up to read in the synagogue as his custom was (Luk 4:16).

“I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren” (1Th 5:27) — one copy, many hearers.
